title: API 653 Training in Mobile, AL: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 653 exam prep for Mobile tank inspectors: Blakeley Island floating-roof tanks, terminal and refinery tank farms, caustic storage. Self-paced online.
h1: API 653 Training in Mobile, Alabama: Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Port Terminals, Refinery Tank Farms and Chemical Storage
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors on Mobile Bay

Crude arrives in the Mobile area by ship and pipeline, products leave by barge, ship and truck, and in between almost all of it sits in aboveground steel tanks. Floating-roof crude and product tanks on Blakeley Island, terminal tankage along the river at Chickasaw, refinery tank farms at Saraland and Pascagoula, and caustic and acid storage in the chemical plants together keep a steady demand for inspectors who can apply API 653. This page is for tank inspectors, terminal maintenance staff, tank welders, coating inspectors and NDT technicians who scan floors and shells and want the certification.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Mobile. The API 653 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions as you go, so a candidate working terminal shifts or travelling between tank jobs can keep studying. API (the American Petroleum Institute) sets eligibility, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and issues the API 653 certification. The course prepares you for that exam; it does not grant certification, and Atlantis is not an API-approved provider.

Tank farms and terminals within reach of Mobile

  • Blakeley Island. When Vertex bought the Mobile refinery from Shell in 2022, the purchase included the Blakeley Island crude and products terminal and about 3.2 million barrels of product storage across the assets. A 2025 operating permit document from the Alabama Department of Environmental Management for Vertex Refining Alabama's Blakeley Island Terminal lists five external floating-roof tanks: four of 9,450,000 gallons, about 225,000 barrels each, and one of 6,300,000 gallons, about 150,000 barrels, each with a metallic shoe primary seal and a rim-mounted secondary seal.
  • World Point's 2014 purchase. When World Point Terminals bought two Mobile terminals from NuStar in 2014, trade press described the Blakeley Island site as 1.182 million barrels of crude, distillate and residual fuel storage served by ship and barge, and the Chickasaw site as 644,000 barrels of asphalt, crude and residual fuel storage with ship, barge, truck and rail access. Terminal ownership changes, so confirm the current operator before you rely on those details.
  • Pascagoula. Chevron says its Pascagoula refinery has more than 300 tanks holding crude, intermediates, finished products and chemicals, some of them above 350,000 barrels, with tank areas built to contain their full capacity. Most of its crude arrives by tanker at the Bayou Casotte marine terminal and is pumped to refinery storage.
  • Chemical storage. Olin's McIntosh plant makes caustic soda, hydrochloric acid and bleach, and the Theodore chemical plants keep raw material and product storage on site. Some of that storage is steel tankage within API 653's scope, and some is lined, alloy or non-metallic construction that the owner manages under other procedures.

Floating roofs, rim seals and heavy rain

A large share of Mobile's petroleum tankage has floating roofs, and that shapes what an inspector spends time on. The roof has to float freely, so pontoons, deck plates, legs and the roof drain all need attention, and the rim seal has to keep vapour in while letting the roof move. The Blakeley Island permit's description of metallic shoe primary seals and rim-mounted secondary seals is a good concrete picture of what the Body of Knowledge means by types of roofs and seals and their deterioration.

Rain is the local complication. Mobile averaged 67.1 inches of precipitation a year over the 1991 to 2020 period, and external floating roofs collect every inch of it. A roof drain that is blocked, jammed by debris or leaking into the product lets water stand on the deck, and standing water adds load the pontoons were not meant to carry. Shell plate under the seal, deck plate around drains and supports, and the drain system itself therefore deserve close inspection on coastal tanks. Wind girders and stairways on large-diameter tanks catch salt and moisture, so atmospheric corrosion on the outside of a coastal tank can be as important as internal attack.

Rules that send a Mobile tank to an API 653 inspector

Most tanks around Mobile reach an API 653 inspector through one of two federal routes, plus whatever the owner's own programme adds.

  • EPA's oil spill prevention rule. Under 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6), facilities with a Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure plan test or inspect each aboveground container for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made. EPA's guidance names API 653 and STI SP001 as the commonly used industry standards; if the plan says a standard will be used, its relevant parts become mandatory. EPA adds that frequent external visual inspections can often be done by trained facility staff, while formal inspections may call for a certified inspector such as an API 653 inspector, and that signed records are kept for at least three years.
  • Pipeline breakout tanks. For hazardous liquid pipeline operators, 49 CFR 195.432 sets three separate requirements. Paragraph (a) requires an inspection of each in-service breakout tank at least once each calendar year and at intervals not exceeding 15 months, except for tanks covered by paragraphs (b) and (c). Paragraph (b) requires atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks to be inspected to API 653, without its risk-based alternative for setting the internal inspection interval. Paragraph (c) sends steel breakout tanks built to API 2510, which is pressurised liquefied gas storage, to section 6 of API 510 instead.

The owner's programme often goes further than either rule, especially at refineries, where tank inspection sits inside the wider mechanical integrity programme. Knowing which rule applies to which tank matters on the job; on the exam, the questions come from API 653 and the documents it references.

The API 653 damage mechanisms, read through local products

The Body of Knowledge for the March 2027 API 653 examination limits RP 571 questions to ten mechanisms. Several match products and conditions found around the bay:

  • Caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking in caustic soda storage, particularly where tanks or their heating coils run warm and welds were not stress relieved.
  • Ethanol stress corrosion cracking in fuel-grade ethanol tanks and blending systems at product terminals.
  • Soil corrosion and concentration cell corrosion on tank bottom undersides, where the foundation, drainage and cathodic protection decide how fast plates thin. RP 651, on cathodic protection of tank bottoms, is in the Body of Knowledge for its sections on corrosion, the need for protection, methods, and operation and maintenance; system design is excluded.
  • Microbiologically influenced corrosion under water bottoms in crude and product tanks.
  • Atmospheric corrosion and corrosion under insulation on shells, roofs and insulated heated tanks, both encouraged by a humid, salty coast.
  • Brittle fracture, which on the coast is mostly a question of hydrostatic testing, reconstruction and the shell material's toughness rather than of winter temperatures.
  • Sulfuric acid corrosion wherever acid is stored or handled.

RP 652, on tank bottom linings, completes the corrosion picture: types of lining, when to recommend one, causes of lining failure and the importance of surface preparation.

Worked example: how far a heavier product lowers the fill height

Changes of service are common at terminals, and the API 653 shell thickness formula answers the question an owner asks first: how high can I fill this tank with the new product? For an entire shell course, t-min = 2.6 (H − 1) D G ÷ (S E), which rearranges to H = S E t ÷ (2.6 D G) + 1.

  1. A 100 ft diameter tank has a lowest average thickness in its bottom course of 0.350 in., determined as API 653 describes. The question gives S = 23,600 psi and E = 1.0.
  2. Present service, a diesel with G = 0.85: H = 23,600 × 1.0 × 0.350 ÷ (2.6 × 100 × 0.85) + 1 = 8,260 ÷ 221 + 1 = 38.4 ft.
  3. Proposed service with G = 1.0: H = 8,260 ÷ 260 + 1 = 32.8 ft.
  4. The heavier product costs about 5.6 ft of fill height on this course alone. Repeat the check for each course above it with its own thickness and its own liquid height, and the lowest permitted level governs.

Two habits prevent most errors: keep H as the height from the bottom of the course being checked, not from the tank bottom, and use the specific gravity of the product actually stored, including any water or heavier fraction the operator expects.

Routes into API 653 for Mobile tank people

Annex D of API 653 sets the eligibility routes, summarised on the API 653 certification requirements page. Experience must be gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency; the length depends on education, from one year with an engineering or technology degree to five or more years without formal education.

  • Tank welders and fitters. Repair, reconstruction and new-bottom work counts toward the longer routes, and the year of inspection experience has to be documented separately.
  • NDT technicians. Floor scanning and shell thickness work is closely related. The current Body of Knowledge does not mention magnetic flux leakage, and its only magnetic method is magnetic particle testing to Section V Article 7 with yokes and prods, so expect questions on API 653's rules for bottom thickness rather than on the scanning technique.
  • Terminal operators and maintenance staff. Hands-on knowledge of roofs, seals, drains and water draws helps a great deal on the job and in the closed-book half, provided your employer can document inspection duties.
  • Coating inspectors. Lining and coating work links directly to RP 652 and to the bottom-side corrosion questions.

Studying API 653 around the terminal year

Tank inspection work arrives unevenly: a tank comes out of service, is cleaned, and then the inspection, repair and return to service run to a tight plan. Self-paced study lets you slow down during that work and catch up afterwards. A sensible order is API 653 first, especially the sections on minimum thickness, settlement, bottom evaluation and repair; then the parts of API 650 the Body of Knowledge includes, which are limited to sections on design metal temperature, materials, reconstruction thickness and weld sizes, NDE, welding and a handful of annex paragraphs; then RP 575, RP 571, RP 577, RP 651 and RP 652, the listed Section V articles and Section IX. Practise the settlement and bottom calculations until they are mechanical, and use the instructor for the questions where API 653 and API 650 seem to say different things.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Mobile terminal or plant

Employers can enrol several candidates together and fees are quoted on request. Terminals with SPCC plans that name API 653 gain from having certified people on staff for the formal inspections, and refineries gain inspectors who can work across their tank fields. Each candidate applies to API individually, and an employer letter that sets out the tanks inspected, the dates and the candidate's role makes the application easier to verify. For technicians who need method training before they move into inspection, see NDT training in Mobile, and for the wider code background read the API 653 tank inspection guide.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in Mobile?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Mobile. The API 653 course is self-paced online, with instructor Q&A when a calculation or clause stalls you, so terminal and refinery staff around Mobile Bay can study between shifts and tank jobs. The examination is in person at a Prometric test centre after API accepts your application, and API issues the certification to those who pass.

faq.q: Does inspection work on the Blakeley Island floating-roof tanks count toward API 653 experience?
faq.a: It can. API counts experience in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of aboveground storage tanks, including the required period of inspection, gained in the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. Describe the tanks, the dates and your duties on the application, and make sure someone who supervised you can confirm them when API verifies the experience.

faq.q: Our terminal's SPCC plan names API 653. Must every tank inspection be done by a certified inspector?
faq.a: Not every one. EPA's guidance says frequent external visual inspections can often be done by trained facility personnel, while formal integrity inspections may require a certified inspector such as an API 653 inspector. Because a standard named in the plan becomes mandatory for its relevant parts, read what API 653 itself requires for each type of inspection and who must perform it, and keep signed records for at least three years.

faq.q: Are pipeline breakout tanks near Mobile inspected differently from terminal tanks?
faq.a: Yes. Under 49 CFR 195.432, atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks are inspected to API 653 but cannot use its risk-based procedure to set the internal inspection interval, and breakout tanks built to API 2510 are inspected to section 6 of API 510. Breakout tanks covered by neither of those paragraphs need an inspection at least each calendar year, with intervals not exceeding 15 months.

faq.q: We store caustic soda. Is caustic damage on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: Yes. The March 2027 Body of Knowledge includes both caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking from RP 571, alongside eight other mechanisms. Learn the critical factors, the affected materials and the inspection methods RP 571 gives for each. Remember that API 653 applies to steel tanks built to API 650 or its predecessor API 12C, so some chemical tanks, such as lined or non-metallic ones, are managed under other procedures.

faq.q: Is MFL floor scanning on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: The current Body of Knowledge does not mention magnetic flux leakage. Floor scanning experience still helps you understand bottom corrosion and can support your experience record, but the exam questions on bottoms come from API 653's rules on minimum remaining thickness, maximum period of operation and the related tables. The NDE content is limited to the Section V articles listed, including magnetic particle testing with yokes and prods.

faq.q: How should I handle API 650 in the open-book half?
faq.a: Only parts of API 650 are examined: design metal temperature, materials and impact testing, reconstructed shell thickness and opening weld sizes, NDE and welding, plus a few annex paragraphs. Bookmark those sections in the PDF and skip the excluded annexes. Many open-book questions ask you to combine API 653's evaluation rules with an API 650 table, so practise moving between the two files quickly.

faq.q: Where can I sit the API 653 exam from Mobile?
faq.a: Prometric lists test centres in and around Mobile, and you choose one when you schedule after API approves your application. The day includes a closed-book part and an open-book part, with the code documents supplied as PDFs on the computer and no personal books allowed. Arrive with the identification Prometric specifies.
